    Weibull regression¶

    Choose the regression parameter¶

    BayesWeibullRegressor supports two models. In both, the selected parameter is exp(intercept + X @ coefficients). The other parameter is shared across observations and sampled in MCMC. Here, “shared” means the same value for all observations; it does not mean a known value held fixed during fitting.

    Model choices¶

    Setting

    Covariates determine

    Shared parameter

    Coefficient interpretation

    regression_parameter="scale"

    Weibull scale

    Weibull shape

    AFT time ratios and constant hazard ratios

    regression_parameter="shape"

    Weibull shape

    Weibull scale

    Changes in the time pattern of risk

    Shape regression remains the default to preserve the existing model. Choose scale regression explicitly when the AFT interpretation fits the application. The choice changes the statistical model, rather than only its notation.

    Scale regression¶

    With shared shape k and scale lambda(x)=exp(intercept + x @ beta), the survival function is

    \[S(t\mid x) = \exp\left[-\left(t/\lambda(x)\right)^k\right].\]

    Increasing one predictor by one unit multiplies every conditional lifetime quantile by exp(beta_j). It also multiplies the mean by that factor. For example, beta_j=log(1.3) gives a 30% increase in median lifetime, with the other predictors held constant. This is an accelerated failure time model.

    The hazard ratio is exp(-k*beta_j) and is constant over time. The Weibull model therefore also has a proportional-hazards interpretation. Its PH coefficient is -k*beta_j, not the AFT coefficient beta_j.

    All observations share the same increasing, decreasing, or constant hazard direction, according to whether k is above, below, or equal to one. Scale regression is a common starting point when covariates act on lifetime. It does not guarantee convergence or precise estimates under heavy censoring.

    Shape regression¶

    With shared scale lambda and shape k(x)=exp(intercept + x @ beta), covariates change how risk evolves over time. Shapes below one give decreasing hazards; shapes above one give increasing hazards.

    All observations have F(lambda)=1-exp(-1): approximately 63.2% have failed at the shared scale. Survival curves with different shapes cross at that time. Their hazards also cross, though generally at another time. These effects do not have constant time-ratio or hazard-ratio interpretations.

    This model can be useful when the scientific hypothesis concerns a change in failure mechanism or wearout pattern. Censoring can make shape effects hard to identify. Estimation also depends on observed failures, covariate support, and priors. Neither model is guaranteed to fail or converge solely because of its parameter choice. This implementation supports right censoring; it does not add left- or interval-censoring support.

    Fit and predict¶

    import numpy as np
from tsdst.estimators import BayesWeibullRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 1))
true_scale = np.exp(1.0 + 0.3*X[:, 0])
lifetime = true_scale*rng.weibull(2.0, size=len(X))
censoring_time = np.full(len(X), 4.0)
time = np.minimum(lifetime, censoring_time)
status = (lifetime <= censoring_time).astype(int)

model = BayesWeibullRegressor(
    regression_parameter="scale",
    shared_prior=(2.0, 1.0),
    niter=10000,
    algo_options={"progress": False},
).fit(X, time, status=status)

mean = model.predict(X)
shape = model.predict_shape(X)
scale = model.predict_scale(X)
variance = model.predict_variance(X)
score = model.score(X, time, scorer="log_likelihood", status=status)

    Shape and scale predictions contain one value per feature row. Mean predictions use the selected coefficient summary and shared parameter; they do not average conditional means over all posterior draws. Use log-likelihood or D2 scoring for censored times. R2 remains the default for complete times.

    The example illustrates the interface. Choose a sufficient chain length and check the actual chain diagnostics for the application.

    Priors and sampled parameters¶

    The intercept has a normal prior with mean zero and standard deviation 10. Slopes have Laplace priors with scale 2*C. With C=None, the existing Weibull implementation uses a fixed slope-prior scale of one.

    shared_prior supplies Gamma shape and scale, in that order:

    • Scale regression defaults to Gamma(2, 1) for the shared Weibull shape.

    • Shape regression keeps Gamma(0.01, 100) for the shared Weibull scale.

    Both hyperparameters must be positive and finite. Their interpretation differs between modes. Weibull scale has time units, while Weibull shape is dimensionless. Changing time units can therefore require changing a prior on shared scale. Review prior sensitivity, particularly when censoring limits the information.

    Each sampled parameter vector contains the intercept and slopes, followed by the log shared parameter. The posterior includes the corresponding log-scale Jacobian. Priors on the coefficients themselves require no additional Jacobian for the regression link.

    shared_parameter_ contains the exponentiated summary of the final log parameter. scale_ is present for shape regression and shape_ is present for scale regression. Use predict_scale and predict_shape for row-wise values in either mode. Changing regression_parameter after fitting requires a new fit; it does not reinterpret the existing chain.

    Comparison with R¶

    For scale regression, R’s survival::survreg(..., dist="weibull") uses the same AFT coefficients. Its reported scale is 1/k, the inverse Weibull shape. Its linear predictor is log Weibull scale. This naming difference must be accounted for when comparing estimates and likelihoods.

    See the R survreg documentation and the NIST Weibull formulas.
